newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto wants dead brother's boydguards arrested.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto wants dead brother's boydguards arrested.

text.p: Pakistani opposition leader Benazir Bhutto said on Saturday authorities should arrest the bodyguards of her dead brother Murtaza, who was killed in mysterious circumstances in a police shootout last year.

In an interview with Reuters, she also demanded that foreign forensic teams join the investigation of the incident, which a judicial tribunal said earlier this month was an "extra-judicial killing" by police cleared by an unspecified higher authority.
Bhutto was prime minister when Murtaza, who was estranged from her and led a breakaway faction of her Pakistan People's Party (PPP), was killed along with seven companions in Karachi on September 20.
At the time Bhutto called the killing a conspiracy to destabilise her government, which was sacked in November by President Farooq Leghari on disputed charges of misrule.

After that, police registered a complaint by Murtaza's widown accusing Bhutto's jailed husband Asif Ali Zardari and the PPP's former chief minister of Sindh province, Abdullah Shah, of involvement in the murder.
Bhutto said in the interview, given on her 44th birthday, that she believed the bodyguards, whom police accuse of starting the shootout, had been bought off.
"I think the bodyguards should be arrested whom the police had accused in their first police report of provocation and starting the firing," Bhutto said.
"Number two, I think forensic experts from abroad should be called in to determine from which angle my brother was actually shot.
"It is very important for the investigation that the bodyguards be arrested, because I believe they were bought off...by my opponents to kill my brother," she said.

The inquiry tribunal report, made public on June 8, exonerated Leghari of Bhutto's suspicion that he was involved in the killing. But it called the incident "a case of extra-judicial killing by the police having clearance from a much higher authority" than Karachi police chiefs.
Bhutto said she believed the report was very important because it "lays to rest" the charge of a conspiracy involving her husband.
"What was so painful for me was not only that my brother was killed but that my husband was accused of that murder," she said.
On Friday, a PPP spokesman said Bhutto had asked party workers not to celebrate her birthday out of respect for her brother.
